desc:
Build an infinite array by writing nums again and again: nums, nums, nums, .... Find the shortest contiguous subarray of this infinite array whose sum is exactly target and return its length, or -1 if no subarray has that sum.

nums = [1, 1, 1, 2], target = 11
infinite array: 1 1 1 2 1 1 1 2 1 1 1 2 ...
[2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2] sums to 11 and has 9 elements
result = 9
hints: The target can be far larger than the sum of one copy of nums, so you cannot materialise the array. How many complete copies must the subarray swallow?

All values are positive, so every n consecutive elements (n = nums.length) sum to total = sum(nums). A subarray covering target // total full cycles uses exactly (target // total) * n elements for that part.

What is left is a remainder target % total that is smaller than one full cycle. Find the shortest subarray with that sum in nums + nums using two pointers (all values positive), and add the two parts.
editorial: Let total be the sum of one copy. Any n consecutive elements sum to exactly total, so a shortest subarray can be viewed as some whole cycles plus a piece shorter than one cycle. Because all numbers are positive, using as many whole cycles as possible, q = target // total, is optimal: each cycle costs n elements, and no shorter way to gain total exists (every element contributes at least 1 and any window of fewer than n elements has a sum below total).

If the remainder r = target % total is 0, the answer is q * n. Otherwise search the shortest subarray of sum exactly r in nums + nums (a subarray shorter than n may wrap around the end). Because all values are positive, a two-pointer window finds it in O(n): grow right, shrink left while the sum exceeds r, and record the length on equality. If none exists the answer is -1; otherwise it is q * n + best. The result is at most target, so it fits in 32 bits.
